claims.text: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys are primarily governed by the density and coherency of nanoscale phase boundaries.
Nanoscale phase boundaries develop during rapid solidification of these alloys.
These nanoscale phase boundaries act as nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transformation.
Changing the distribution of nanoscale phase boundaries will change both hysteresis and the breadth of the entropy-change profile during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy has a single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Laser surface remelting followed by rapid resolidification will refine the surface microstructure.
Laser surface remelting will increase the density of nanoscale phase boundaries.
Increasing the density of coherent nanoscale phase boundaries lowers the energy barriers for the magnetostructural transformation.
Lower transformation barriers reduce kinetic hysteresis.
Increasing coherent phase-boundary density broadens the temperature range over which the magnetostructural transition occurs.
The refined microstructure produces a more continuous and reversible phase transformation.
A more continuous and reversible phase transformation enhances magnetocaloric performance for rapid heat exchange.
Laser-treated samples will show a less abrupt transition than the as-deposited controls.
Laser-treated samples will show reduced hysteresis relative to the as-deposited controls.
Laser-treated samples will show a broadened entropy-change profile relative to the as-deposited controls.
The overall entropy-change magnitude may remain high after laser treatment.
The predicted effects apply near the transition temperature at applied magnetic fields below 1 T.
Thermal stresses induced by laser remelting may compete with the proposed beneficial microstructural effects.

contradictions.description: The initial alloy is described as single-phase hexagonal, while the proposed governing feature is a pre-existing density of nanoscale phase boundaries developed during rapid solidification. A strictly single-phase state cannot contain phase boundaries unless additional phases or transformation interfaces are identified; the alternative phrase 'interfacial regions' does not resolve which interface is meant.
